dialogue.text: [calm, ominous] Day one. The whole world wakes up to a normal Monday. In Tokyo it's almost midnight, in London people are coming back from lunch, and in New York the stock market is about to open. And by the end of today, the world economy will have started to fall apart.

[calm, ominous] By the end of this story, a few countries will be in ruins, you'll find out whether the money in your account is still worth anything, and one country will be sitting on top of the pile, writing the new rules for everybody else. Which country that is, and why, is the strangest part of the whole thing.
[calm] The company that starts it is made up. But every step after it has really happened somewhere before, and a lot of it happened this year.

[serious, engaging] And the world is already on edge. A war with Iran kept tankers out of the Strait of Hormuz for months this year, so filling up a car costs more than it did last winter. Interest rates in America just went up for the first time in three years, so every loan costs more. And tech companies have borrowed almost five hundred billion dollars this year alone to build AI data centers.

[serious, engaging] One of those borrowers is a company called Corvane. It owns a giant warehouse in Virginia full of AI chips and rents them out to AI companies. To buy them, it borrowed twelve billion dollars, and promised the lenders they could take the chips if Corvane ever stopped paying.

[serious, engaging] At 10:17 on Monday morning, a four-hundred-million-dollar payment from Corvane fails to arrive at its bank. Its biggest customer, an AI lab that has never made a profit, stopped paying its bills on Friday.

[serious, engaging] So the lenders come for the chips, and that's when everyone finds out what those chips are really worth. On paper, forty thousand dollars each. At a fire sale, with every lender selling at once, maybe five.
